mcqs.question: A developer adds `role="button"` to a `<div>` in a spot where `<button>` would work identically. What does the WAI-ARIA spec's own guidance say about this?
options: It's the recommended pattern, since ARIA is designed to replace native elements wherever possible
It's only a problem if the div is missing a tabindex attribute
It's required whenever a div needs to be styled as a button for visual consistency
It's a violation of ARIA's own first rule — a native element should always be used over an ARIA-patched generic one when it covers the same case
mcqs.explanation: The WAI-ARIA spec explicitly states "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" and that native elements should be used first whenever they cover the needed behavior — reaching for ARIA when a native element would work identically is precisely the pattern this rule warns against. ARIA isn't meant to replace native elements generally, and adding tabindex alone wouldn't fix the deeper issue of using the wrong element to begin with.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a state, as distinct from a role or a property, and why does that category matter?
options: aria-expanded, because it reflects the current condition of a toggle and must be kept updated as that condition changes
role="dialog", because it needs to be recalculated every time the dialog's content changes
aria-label, because it changes dynamically every time the component re-renders
aria-describedby, because it represents the element's core identity
mcqs.explanation: aria-expanded is the textbook example of a state — it describes a current, changeable condition and must be kept in sync with the real UI, unlike a role (set once, rarely changes) or most properties. role="dialog" doesn't need recalculation as content changes, and aria-label/aria-describedby aren't inherently dynamic just by being properties.

mcqs.question: A custom tab interface uses `role="tablist"`, `role="tab"`, and `role="tabpanel"` but never sets `aria-selected` on any tab. What's wrong with this implementation?
options: Nothing — aria-selected is optional decoration for tab interfaces
The roles should be replaced entirely since tabs require a native HTML element instead
aria-selected only matters if the tabs are keyboard-operable
The roles are incomplete without aria-selected, since each role comes with an implicit contract for the states that must accompany it
mcqs.explanation: Roles carry an implicit contract for which states/properties must accompany them, and role="tab" without aria-selected anywhere is an incomplete implementation, not a minimal valid one — a screen reader has no way to announce which tab is currently active. There's no native tabs element to fall back to instead, and aria-selected matters regardless of keyboard operability.

mcqs.question: A modal sets `aria-hidden="true"` on the rest of the page's content while it's open, which is correct. What's the dangerous mistake to avoid regarding this same attribute?
options: Forgetting to remove aria-hidden from the rest of the page after the modal closes, which makes the entire page invisible to a screen reader with no visual sign anything is wrong
Applying aria-hidden to the modal itself instead of the background content
Using aria-hidden instead of the CSS display property
Setting aria-hidden before the modal has finished its opening animation
mcqs.explanation: The real-world failure mode is state going stale in the other direction — leaving aria-hidden="true" on the background after the modal closes silently blocks a screen reader user from the entire rest of the page, with nothing visually indicating the problem. Applying it to the background while the modal is open is the correct pattern, not a mistake, and this issue is unrelated to CSS display or animation timing specifically.

mcqs.question: A custom checkbox is built with `role="checkbox"` and `aria-checked` on a `<div>`, with click and keydown handlers added manually. Compared to `<input type="checkbox">`, what's the actual cost of this approach?
options: There is no real cost — both approaches are functionally identical once the ARIA attributes are added

The custom version requires manually implementing and maintaining everything the native checkbox provides for free — role, keyboard handling for both click and key activation, and updating the checked state on every toggle
The custom version is more accessible because it gives finer control over styling
The only cost is a slightly larger HTML payload
mcqs.explanation: Every piece of behavior in the custom implementation — role, focusability, key handling, and state tracking — is something the native checkbox provides automatically and correctly; the custom version has to reimplement and keep all of it correct as the component changes, a real ongoing cost. Styling flexibility doesn't require abandoning the native element, and the meaningful cost here is maintenance risk, not payload size.

mcqs.question: A dropdown can be closed either by clicking its trigger or by clicking outside it. The outside-click handler was added later and never updates `aria-expanded`. What's the correct fix?
options: Add a periodic check that polls aria-expanded and corrects it every few seconds
Remove aria-expanded entirely since it's clearly unreliable
Route every code path that changes the open/closed state through one shared function that updates both the visual state and aria-expanded together
Only worry about it since automated accessibility scanners will catch the mismatch
mcqs.explanation: The real fix is architectural — centralizing every state-changing path through one function so the ARIA attribute can never drift from the visual state, rather than patching each new close path individually as bugs surface. Polling is a workaround that masks the root cause, removing the attribute loses real accessibility information, and automated scanners generally can't detect this kind of state-sync staleness from a static snapshot.
